sentences.text: Here are our 103 patients. They fit on one laptop, with plenty of room to spare.
Now picture a national registry: every patient, every visit, for years.
The laptop's memory fills, and then it overflows. One machine isn't enough.
So we spread the work across many machines. But then, which machine does what?
Welcome to Spark, Visually.
Today: who does the work.
Let's build the cluster, piece by piece. At the bottom: storage. Our cast is written there as 4 files.
Above it, four machines, called workers. On each one runs a process called an executor.
Each executor has cores, and a core runs one task at a time. 4 executors with 2 cores each: 8 tasks can run at once.
And above them all, the driver. It holds the Spark session, plans the work and hands it out.
The executors were started by the cluster manager, when the driver asked for them.
On a classic cluster, your notebook's Python runs on the driver machine itself.
On some Databricks compute, it doesn't. With Spark Connect, the notebook is a small client: it sends each query to a driver on the cluster, and gets back only the result.
Everything in this series runs both ways. What doesn't run on Spark Connect is the old, low-level route through the SparkContext, like df.rdd. So we won't use it.
Now, some code. Line one reads our table.
It returns at once, and nothing moves. No machine touches a single row. We'll see why in episode 3.
Line two counts the rows.
The driver turns that into 4 tasks, one for each file, and sends them down to the executors.
Each executor reads its own file, straight from storage. The data never passes through the driver.
Each task counts its own rows: 28, 25, 25 and 25.
The 4 partial counts go to one final task, which adds them up. And just one number goes up to the driver: 103.
Line three asks for every row: collect.
Now all 103 patients travel up to the driver.
For our cast, that's nothing. Now make it 10,000 times bigger: about a million rows.
Count still sends up one number. Collect lands every row on the driver: over 500 megabytes of memory.
For a whole registry, that would swamp the driver. Rows should stay down, with the executors.
One more surprise. The Python you write mostly just builds a plan.
The real work, reading, counting, adding, runs inside the executors, in Java, not Python.
Unless you write your own Python function, a UDF. Then each executor starts Python workers beside it, and ships the rows out to them in batches, and back.
That takes time, and Spark can't see inside your function.
Let's gather it up.
The driver plans the work and hands out tasks.
The executors read the data, and do the work.
And rows stay down, unless you ask for them.
One loose end: our count read the table with 4 tasks, but we have 8 cores.
Why only four? Next time: piles of records.
This has been Spark, Visually. Thanks for watching the cluster with us.
